title: How Sound Travels
summary: How vibrations make sound, how sound waves move through air, water, and solids but not through space, and how pitch, echoes, and our ears work.
poll: Sound can travel anywhere, even through outer space.

versions.title: How Sound Moves
versions.text:
Hit a drum. Boom! The top of the drum shakes. It moves back and forth fast. We say it vibrates.

All sounds start this way. Each sound comes from a thing that vibrates.

The drum pushes on the air. The air bumps the air next to it. The push moves on and on. This is a sound wave.

Sound can move through air. It can move through water. It can move through walls, too. It moves fast in water. It moves even faster in hard things.

In space there is no air. So there is no sound there. Space is still and quiet.

Light is much faster than sound. In a storm, you see the flash first. Then you hear the thunder.

Some sounds are high. Some are low. This is called pitch. Fast shakes make a high pitch. Slow shakes make a low pitch.

Sound can bounce off a cliff. Then you hear it two times. That is an echo. Bats use echoes to find bugs at night.

The wave goes in your ear. It hits a thin skin. That is your eardrum. It shakes, too. Your brain hears the sound.

Out in space, there is no air. So sound cannot move there. Space is silent.

Light moves much faster than sound. In a storm, you see the flash first. Then you hear the thunder a bit later.

Some sounds are high, like a bird. Some are low, like a big drum. How high or low a sound is is called its pitch. Fast shakes make a high pitch, and slow shakes make a low pitch.

Sound can bounce off a hard wall or a cliff. Then you hear it again. That is called an echo. Bats make sounds and listen for echoes. This helps them find bugs in the dark.

The sound wave goes into your ear. It hits a thin skin called the eardrum. The eardrum shakes, too. Then your brain tells you what you hear.

versions.title: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
Tap a drum and listen. Boom! When you hit the drum, its top shakes back and forth very fast. We say that it vibrates.

Every sound begins this way. A guitar string, a bell, and even your own voice all make sound because something vibrates.

When the drum vibrates, it pushes on the air next to it. That air bumps into the air beside it. The push keeps moving. This traveling push is called a sound wave.

Sound waves can move through air. They can also move through water and through solid things like walls and the ground. Sound travels faster in water than in air. It travels even faster through solid steel.

In outer space, there is no air. Sound has nothing to move through, so space is completely silent.

Light travels much faster than sound. During a storm, you see the lightning first. You hear the thunder a few seconds later.

Some sounds are high, like a small bird. Others are low, like a big drum. How high or low a sound is is called its pitch. Fast vibrations make a high pitch. Slow vibrations make a low pitch.

Sound can bounce off a hard wall or a cliff. When it comes back to you, you hear an echo. Bats make squeaks and listen for echoes. This helps them find insects in the dark.

When a sound wave reaches you, it goes into your ear. It makes a thin piece of skin called the eardrum vibrate. Then your brain turns the message into a sound you can understand.

versions.title: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
Hit a drum, and you will hear a loud boom. At the moment you strike it, the tight top of the drum shakes back and forth very quickly. Scientists say that it vibrates.

Every sound begins with something that vibrates. A plucked string, a ringing bell, and even your own voice all make sound in this way. When you speak, small parts inside your throat vibrate.

As the drum vibrates, it pushes on the air beside it. That air pushes on the air next to it, and the push keeps passing along. This traveling push is called a sound wave.

Sound waves can travel through air, through water, and through solid things such as wood, walls, and the ground. Sound moves about four times faster in water than in air. It moves even faster through solid steel.

In outer space, there is almost no air. Sound has nothing to travel through, so space is silent.

Light travels much faster than sound. During a storm, you see a flash of lightning first and hear the thunder a few seconds later.

Some sounds are high, like a whistle. Others are low, like a large drum. How high or low a sound is is called its pitch. Fast vibrations make a high pitch, and slow vibrations make a low pitch.

Sound can bounce off a hard surface, such as a cliff. When it comes back, you hear an echo. Bats make squeaks and listen for echoes to find insects in the dark.

When a sound wave enters your ear, it makes your eardrum vibrate. Your brain then turns the message into a sound you understand.

versions.title: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
When you strike a drum, you hear a deep boom. At that instant, the tight skin on top of the drum moves back and forth very quickly. This rapid shaking is called a vibration. It is where every sound begins.

A plucked string, a ringing bell, and a buzzing bee all make sound because something is vibrating. When you talk, small folds inside your throat vibrate as air from your lungs passes over them.

Air is made of tiny particles that are far too small to see. When the drum skin pushes outward, it squeezes the air particles beside it. Those particles bump into their neighbors, and the push passes along from particle to particle. This traveling disturbance is a sound wave.

The material that a sound wave travels through is called a medium. Air is one medium. Water and solids such as wood and stone work as well. Sound moves about four times faster in water than in air, and it moves even faster through steel.

In outer space there is almost no air, so it is close to a vacuum. With no particles to pass the wave along, sound cannot travel, and space is silent.

Light travels far faster than sound. That is why, during a storm, you see the lightning before you hear the thunder.

The number of vibrations each second is called the frequency. A high frequency makes a high pitch, and a low frequency makes a low pitch.

Sound can also bounce off hard surfaces and return as an echo. Bats and dolphins send out sounds and listen for the echoes. This helps them find food. This skill is called echolocation.

When a sound wave enters your ear, it makes your eardrum vibrate. Tiny parts inside your ear pass the vibration along, and your brain turns it into a sound you understand.

versions.title: Waves You Can Hear: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
When a drummer strikes a drum, a deep, booming sound fills the room almost instantly. At that moment, the tightly stretched skin on top of the drum moves back and forth extremely rapidly, and this rapid shaking, which scientists call a vibration, is the origin of every sound we hear, from a gentle whisper to a roaring thunderclap.

A plucked guitar string, a ringing bell, and a buzzing mosquito all generate sound because something is vibrating. Even when you speak, delicate folds of tissue in your throat vibrate as air from your lungs rushes between them.

Air consists of tiny particles that are far too small to observe. When the drum skin pushes outward, it squeezes the neighboring air particles closer together, forming a region of high pressure called a compression. When the skin moves back, it leaves a region where the particles are spread farther apart. These alternating zones travel outward from particle to particle, similar to people in a line passing along a message, and together they form a sound wave.

The material that a sound wave travels through is called its medium. Air is the most familiar medium, but water and solid materials such as wood, stone, and metal also transmit sound. Because their particles are packed more closely together, sound travels approximately four times faster in water than in air, and it travels considerably faster still through steel.

Outer space is nearly a vacuum, meaning that it contains almost no particles, so sound cannot travel there, and even an enormous explosion in space would be completely silent.

Light travels tremendously faster than sound, which explains why, during a thunderstorm, you observe the lightning flash before you hear the thunder.

The number of vibrations each second is called the frequency. It determines the pitch: a high frequency produces a high pitch, whereas a low frequency produces a low, rumbling one. The strength of the vibration, called its amplitude, determines loudness, which scientists measure in units called decibels.

Sound can also reflect off hard surfaces and return to the listener as an echo. Bats and dolphins emit sounds and listen attentively for the returning echoes, which helps them locate food, an ability known as echolocation.

When a sound wave reaches your ear, it causes your eardrum to vibrate. Three tiny bones transfer the vibration to the cochlea, a fluid-filled, snail-shaped part of the inner ear, and your brain ultimately interprets the signal as a recognizable sound.

versions.title: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
Sound is a form of energy that travels outward through the air, and indeed through many other substances as well, in the form of invisible waves. Whenever any object vibrates rapidly back and forth, it pushes against the surrounding air molecules, creating alternating regions of compression, where the molecules are squeezed tightly together, and rarefaction, where they are spread considerably farther apart. These alternating regions travel outward from the source in every direction, forming what scientists call a sound wave, which eventually reaches a listener's ear and is subsequently interpreted by the brain as a recognizable sound.

The particular pitch of any sound, meaning how high or low it registers to a listener, depends directly on its frequency, which refers precisely to how many complete wave cycles occur within a single second. A sound wave with a high frequency produces a correspondingly high-pitched sound, such as a bird's piercing chirp, whereas a wave with a low frequency produces a deep, low-pitched sound, such as distant rolling thunder. The loudness of any sound, by contrast, depends instead on its amplitude, which describes precisely how much the air pressure actually changes as the wave passes through a given point in space. A larger amplitude reliably produces a louder sound, and loudness itself is commonly measured in units called decibels.

Sound requires some physical medium, whether solid, liquid, or gaseous, through which to travel from its source to a listener; it cannot propagate at all through the complete vacuum of outer space, since there are no particles present there to compress and transmit the resulting vibration onward. Sound actually travels considerably faster through solids and liquids than it does through ordinary air. The particles in these denser substances are packed much more closely together and can transmit vibrations between neighboring particles far more efficiently and quickly than the comparatively sparse molecules of air can manage.

When a sound wave eventually reaches the human ear, it first causes the eardrum, a thin and remarkably sensitive membrane, to vibrate sympathetically in response. These vibrations are then transmitted mechanically through three tiny interconnected bones in the middle ear before finally reaching the cochlea, a small spiral-shaped structure filled with fluid that converts these physical vibrations into electrical nerve signals that the brain can readily interpret as meaningful sound.

Sound also readily reflects off hard, solid surfaces, producing the familiar phenomenon known as an echo whenever the reflected sound returns to a listener's ear after a perceptible, measurable delay. This same essential principle underlies sonar technology. Ships and submarines use to detect underwater objects, and it likewise explains why an empty, unfurnished room typically sounds noticeably different, often harsher and more reverberant, than one filled with soft, sound-absorbing furniture.

In the markets and mosques of Saudi Arabia, the human voice travels effectively through open desert air across considerable distances. Inside enclosed stone buildings, sound waves reflect repeatedly off hard surfaces, creating the rich, lingering echoes and natural reverberation long associated architecturally with traditional mosque design and construction throughout the region.

versions.title: How Sound Travels
versions.text:
Sound is a genuine form of physical energy that travels outward continuously through the air, and indeed through many other substances as well, in the form of invisible, propagating waves. Whenever any object vibrates rapidly back and forth at sufficient speed, it pushes forcefully against the surrounding air molecules, creating alternating regions of compression, where the molecules are squeezed tightly together, and rarefaction, where those same molecules are instead spread considerably farther apart from one another. These alternating regions of compressed and rarefied air travel outward from their point of origin in every direction simultaneously, forming what scientists technically call a sound wave, which eventually reaches a listener's ear and is subsequently interpreted by the brain as a recognizable, meaningful sound.

The particular pitch of any given sound, meaning precisely how high or low it registers subjectively to a listener, depends directly on its frequency, which refers specifically to how many complete wave cycles occur within a single second of elapsed time. A sound wave characterized by a high frequency reliably produces a correspondingly high-pitched sound, such as a bird's piercing chirp overhead, whereas a wave characterized instead by a low frequency produces a deep, low-pitched sound, such as distant rolling thunder on the horizon. The loudness of any given sound, by clear contrast, depends instead on its amplitude, which describes precisely how much the local air pressure actually fluctuates as the wave passes through any particular point in space. A larger amplitude reliably produces a correspondingly louder sound overall, and loudness itself is conventionally measured using units called decibels.

Sound fundamentally requires some physical medium, whether solid, liquid, or gaseous in its nature, through which to travel continuously from its original source all the way to a listener; it simply cannot propagate at all through the complete vacuum of outer space, since there are no particles present there whatsoever to compress, rarefy, and thereby transmit the resulting vibration onward through the emptiness. Sound actually travels considerably faster through solids and liquids than it does through ordinary air, because the constituent particles within these denser substances are packed much more closely together and can therefore transmit vibrations between adjacent particles far more efficiently and rapidly than the comparatively sparse, widely spaced molecules of ordinary air can ever manage to achieve.

When a sound wave eventually reaches the human ear after traveling through the air, it first causes the eardrum, a thin and remarkably sensitive membrane, to vibrate sympathetically in direct response to the incoming pressure changes. These resulting vibrations are then transmitted mechanically through three tiny, interconnected bones located within the middle ear before finally reaching the cochlea, a small spiral-shaped structure filled entirely with fluid that reliably converts these physical vibrations into electrical nerve signals that the brain can then readily interpret as meaningful, recognizable sound.

Sound also readily reflects off hard, solid surfaces of various kinds, producing the familiar phenomenon widely known as an echo whenever the reflected sound wave returns to a listener's ear after a perceptible, measurable time delay. This same essential underlying principle forms the basis of sonar technology, which ships and submarines routinely use to detect submerged objects and navigate safely underwater, and it likewise explains convincingly why an empty, unfurnished room typically sounds noticeably different, often considerably harsher and more reverberant, than an otherwise identical room filled instead with soft, sound-absorbing furniture and fabric.

In the bustling markets and historic mosques of Saudi Arabia, the human voice travels remarkably effectively through open desert air across quite considerable distances, while inside enclosed stone buildings constructed with hard, reflective surfaces, sound waves instead reflect repeatedly off walls and ceilings, creating the rich, lingering echoes and natural architectural reverberation that have long been associated with traditional mosque design and construction practices throughout the broader region.

keyWords.definition: to shake back and forth very fast
keyWords.example: My phone began to vibrate on the table when my aunt called.

keyWords.definition: a push or movement that travels from one place to another
keyWords.example: A wave of cheers moved across the crowd at the match.

keyWords.definition: how high or low a sound is
keyWords.example: The little whistle made a sound with a very high pitch.

keyWords.definition: a sound that bounces back so you hear it again

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a drum at home
How sound is made, how it moves, and how we hear it
Why storms are dangerous
How bats catch bugs
questions.why: The whole article explains that sound starts with something that vibrates, moves as a wave, and is heard by our ears.

wrong.A: A drum is used as an example, but the article does not teach how to build one.
wrong.C: Storms are mentioned only to show that light is faster than sound.
wrong.D: Bats are one small example of echoes, not the main topic.

questions.stem: How does every sound begin?
options: With light that shines from the sun
With air that stays very still
With something that vibrates
With a loud storm
questions.why: The article says every sound starts with a thing that vibrates, or shakes back and forth fast.

wrong.A: Light is not how sound begins.
wrong.B: Sound happens when air is pushed and moves, not when it stays still.
wrong.D: Thunder is one sound, but not every sound comes from a storm.

questions.stem: Why is there no sound in space?
options: There is no air for sound to move through.
Space is much too cold for any sound.
Space is too dark for anyone to hear.
The stars in space are too far away.
questions.why: The article says there is no air in space, so sound has nothing to move through.

wrong.B: The article does not say cold stops sound.
wrong.C: Darkness has nothing to do with hearing.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about how far the stars are.

questions.stem: Through which of these does sound move the fastest?
options: Air
Water in a lake
Empty outer space
Hard things like steel
questions.why: The article says sound moves faster in water than in air, and even faster in hard things like steel.

wrong.A: Sound is slowest in air of the three.
wrong.B: Water is faster than air, but hard things are faster still.
wrong.C: Sound cannot move through empty space at all.

questions.stem: In the article, the word pitch means —

how high or low a sound is
the place where a sound starts
a sound that comes back

wrong.D: A sound that comes back is an echo.

wrong.C: Bird songs travel through air to our ears.
wrong.D: An echo is a sound that bounces back. A bird's song is not always an echo.

wrong.B: The article does not say clouds block sound.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about ears being slow.

MID.modelAnswer: I see lightning before I hear thunder because light travels enormously faster than sound does, so the flash reaches my eyes long before the rumble reaches my ears. Sound needs a medium, like air, water, or metal, made of particles that can bump into each other and carry the sound wave along. Space, however, is nearly a vacuum with almost no particles at all, so there is nothing to pass the vibration from place to place, which is why space is completely silent. This is very different from animals like bats, which use echolocation and depend on a medium full of particles to send out sounds and listen for their echoes.

HIGH.prompt: Compare frequency and amplitude. Explain what each one changes about a sound, and give an example of each.
checklist: I explained that frequency changes pitch.
I explained that amplitude changes loudness and is measured in decibels.
I gave a clear example for each one.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Frequency and amplitude are two different properties of a sound wave, and each one changes something different about what we hear. Frequency measures how many times the wave's compression repeats each second as it is transmitted through the air, and a higher frequency produces a higher pitch, like a bird's chirp, while a lower frequency produces a lower pitch, like a deep drum. Amplitude, on the other hand, describes how large the wave itself is, which determines loudness measured in decibels, so a gentle whisper has low amplitude while a shouting crowd has very high amplitude. Once these vibrations reach the cochlea inside the ear, the brain interprets frequency as pitch and amplitude as volume, allowing us to tell a quiet high note apart from a loud low one.
